extracted.intended_audience: members of the public, stakeholders, businesses, and advocacy groups interested in participating in FTC Section 18 rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for members of the public and stakeholders on how to participate in the Federal Trade Commission’s Section 18 notice-and-comment rulemaking process, what to include in comments, when to submit them, and other participation options (petitions, rebuttals, hearings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunities to weigh in (stages)
rubrics_metrics.description: You have three opportunities to weigh in by: 1. responding to an Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking; 2. responding to a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking; and 3. presenting your views at an 'informal hearing,' if a hearing is held and you request to speak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During the process, commenters with specific factual disputes may submit rebuttal comments or conduct cross-examination at informal hearings. The booklet emphasizes these distinct windows as the primary moments to provide input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing a petition for rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have an idea for a rule but the FTC hasn’t asked about it in a notice, the FTC accepts and reviews petitions for rulemaking from the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you file a qualifying petition it will be posted for members of the public to provide comments about it. The booklet points readers to additional resources (go.usa.gov/xumtG) for how to file a petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include additional information, data, experiences, perspectives, or arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: An effective comment gives additional information, data, experiences, perspectives, or arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The booklet notes that these substantive contributions are what help the FTC understand the effects of a proposed rule. It implies preference for concrete evidence or firsthand experience over unsupported assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address the notice’s specific questions
rubrics_metrics.description: A comment addressing one or more of the specific questions posed in the FTC’s notice is particularly helpful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because notices typically ask targeted questions about a proposed rule and its effect, tying your comment directly to those questions makes it more useful to agency decision-makers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format and length flexibility (tone and formality)
rubrics_metrics.description: A comment doesn’t need to be long or formal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The booklet reassures the public that effective comments can be concise and need not follow a formal legal brief format—focus on helpful information rather than length or formality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may submit comments
rubrics_metrics.description: You can submit a comment on behalf of yourself, a group, or a business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guidance affirms that individuals, organizations, and commercial entities all may participate and that perspectives from any of these sources are considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the NPRM’s contents (proposed text and reasoning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Typically, the FTC publishes a notice with the proposed text of the rule that explains the agency’s reasoning and asks the public to submit comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments should consider the proposed text and the agency’s stated reasoning—suggested better approaches that respond to the proposal and rationale are expressly noted as potentially influential on the agency’s final decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public comments are considered and can change outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Public comments are an important way for the FTC to hear directly from affected people and communities; the FTC reads and considers all comments when deciding what to do next—and could decide that you suggested a better approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This underscores that substantive, well-targeted comments can meaningfully affect the agency’s decision; the booklet encourages participation by explaining the potential impact of comments.
